title: Νεκροὶ καὶ τεῖχος
titleEn: The Dead and the Wall — Iliad 7.379–482
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Idaeus goes at dawn to the Achaean assembly by Agamemnon’s ship and delivers Priam’s two messages: Paris will give back the goods he brought from Argos, with more besides, but not Helen, though the Trojans urge him to; and the Trojans ask a truce to burn the dead. Diomedes answers that no one should take the goods or Helen, since the offer itself shows the Trojans are doomed, and the army shouts its assent. Agamemnon grants the truce and calls Zeus to witness. Both sides gather their dead at sunrise, wash them, weep, and burn them. Before the next dawn the Achaeans raise one mound over the pyre and build a wall with towers, gates and a staked ditch. Poseidon complains to Zeus that the wall will outshine the one he and Apollo built for Laomedon; Zeus tells him to wash it into the sea once the Achaeans sail home. The sun sets, wine-ships come from Lemnos, both armies feast all night, and Zeus thunders over them until they pour libations and sleep.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδ’ ἐπίθοντο·
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara tou mala men klyon ēd’ epithonto·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed;
sentences.n: Priam has just finished giving his orders for the night (the end of the previous part), and the Trojans obey. The line is a stock close to a speech and keeps the Odyssey’s English for it. ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο ‘he spoke’ with its last vowel dropped and τ made θ before the rough breathing of οἳ; οἳ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and they then’, the article as a pronoun. κλύον is an unaugmented aorist of κλύω ‘hear’, taking the genitive τοῦ ‘him’, and ἐπίθοντο the aorist middle of πείθω, ‘obeyed’; μάλα μέν ‘readily’ strengthens the first verb. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: δόρπον ἔπειθ’ εἵλοντο κατὰ στρατὸν ἐν τελέεσσιν·
sentences.tr: dorpon epeith’ heilonto kata straton en teleessin·
sentences.l: supper then they took throughout the army, in their companies;
sentences.i: then they took their supper throughout the army, company by company;
sentences.n: The Trojans’ evening. δόρπον is ‘supper’, the evening meal, the word Priam used at 370; ἔπειθ’ is ἔπειτα ‘then’ elided, and εἵλοντο the aorist middle of αἱρέω, ‘took’. κατὰ στρατόν is ‘throughout the army’, the Trojan force, which Priam at 370 sent to its supper through the city. ἐν τελέεσσιν is the epic dative plural of τέλος, which here means a ‘company’, a division of troops, a sense the word has only in such phrases; its usual meaning is ‘end, fulfilment’.

sentences.t: ἠῶθεν δ’ Ἰδαῖος ἔβη κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας·
sentences.tr: ēōthen d’ Idaios ebē koilas epi nēas·
sentences.l: and at dawn Idaeus went to the hollow ships;
sentences.i: and at dawn Idaeus went to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: The herald sets out as Priam ordered at 372, and the line repeats that order with ἔβη ‘went’, an unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, in place of ἴτω ‘let him go’. ἠῶθεν is ‘at dawn’, ἠώς ‘dawn’ with the suffix -θεν, which usually means ‘from’ and here marks the time. κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας is ‘to the hollow ships’, the stock epithet translated as always.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ εὗρ’ εἰν ἀγορῇ Δαναοὺς θεράποντας Ἄρηος
νηῒ πάρα πρύμνῃ Ἀγαμέμνονος·
sentences.tr:
tous d’ heur’ ein agorēi Danaous therapontas Arēos
nēï para prymnēi Agamemnonos·
sentences.l:
and them he found in assembly, the Danaans, attendants of Ares,
beside the stern of Agamemnon’s ship;
sentences.i: and he found them in assembly, the Danaans, attendants of Ares, beside the stern of Agamemnon’s ship;
sentences.n: The Achaeans are already met. τούς ‘them’ is the article as a pronoun, explained by Δαναούς; εὗρ’ is εὗρε, an unaugmented aorist of εὑρίσκω ‘find’, and εἰν is ἐν with its vowel lengthened for the metre. Δαναοὺς θεράποντας Ἄρηος ‘Danaans, attendants of Ares’ is the stock phrase for the army as fighting men, θεράπων being one who serves a greater man. νηῒ πάρα πρύμνῃ is ‘beside the stern of the ship’, with πάρα after its noun and the dative πρύμνῃ ‘stern’ agreeing with νηΐ; the leaders meet by Agamemnon’s ship. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 383.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ τοῖσι
στὰς ἐν μέσσοισιν μετεφώνεεν ἠπύτα κῆρυξ·
sentences.tr:
autar ho toisi
stas en messoisin metephōneen ēpyta kēryx·
sentences.l:
but he, to them,
standing in their midst, spoke among them, the loud-voiced herald:
sentences.i: But the loud-voiced herald, standing in their midst, spoke among them:
sentences.n: Idaeus speaks to the gathered Achaeans. ὅ is the article as a pronoun, ‘he’, named only at the end of the next line as ἠπύτα κῆρυξ ‘the loud-voiced herald’: ἠπύτα is a masculine adjective in -α (like ἱππότα), from ἠπύω ‘call aloud’. στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι ‘stand’, and ἐν μέσσοισιν ‘in the midst’ is the speaker’s place in an assembly. μετεφώνεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of μεταφωνέω ‘speak among’, with τοῖσι ‘to them’ as its dative; the literal layer keeps both words for ‘among’.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη τε καὶ ἄλλοι ἀριστῆες Παναχαιῶν
ἠνώγει Πρίαμός τε καὶ ἄλλοι Τρῶες ἀγαυοὶ
εἰπεῖν, αἴ κέ περ ὔμμι φίλον καὶ ἡδὺ γένοιτο,
μῦθον Ἀλεξάνδροιο, τοῦ εἵνεκα νεῖκος ὄρωρε·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē te kai alloi aristēes Panachaiōn
ēnōgei Priamos te kai alloi Trōes agauoi
eipein, ai ke per ymmi philon kai hēdy genoito,
mython Alexandroio, tou heineka neikos orōre·
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, and you other best men of the Achaeans all together,
Priam bade me, and the other Trojans, noble ones,
to tell, if to you it should be dear and sweet,
the word of Alexander, for whose sake the quarrel has arisen;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, and you other best men of all the Achaeans, Priam and the other noble Trojans have bidden me tell you, if it should be dear and sweet to you, the word of Alexander, for whose sake the quarrel has arisen;
sentences.n: Idaeus opens with the address Nestor used at 327 and delivers Priam’s first message, closing with the line Priam spoke at 374; both lines keep their English. ἠνώγει is the pluperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, used as a past tense; it is singular, agreeing with the nearer subject Πρίαμος, though ἄλλοι Τρῶες ἀγαυοί ‘the other noble Trojans’ share in the bidding; the ‘me’ is understood. εἰπεῖν ‘to tell’ takes μῦθον ‘the word’ as its object. αἴ κέ περ … γένοιτο is ‘if it should be’, with ὔμμι the Aeolic dative ‘to you’ and φίλον καὶ ἡδύ ‘dear and sweet’. ὄρωρε is the perfect of ὄρνυμι, ‘has arisen’. Idaeus’s speech begins.

sentences.t:
κτήματα μὲν ὅσ’ Ἀλέξανδρος κοίλῃς ἐνὶ νηυσὶν
ἠγάγετο Τροίηνδ’·
sentences.tr:
ktēmata men hos’ Alexandros koilēis eni nēusin
ēgageto Troiēnd’·
sentences.l:
The possessions, for one, as many as Alexander in hollow ships
brought to Troy—
sentences.i: The possessions that Alexander brought to Troy in his hollow ships—
sentences.n: The offer begins with its object, and the verb that governs it waits until 391; the dash marks the break where a wish cuts in. κτήματα μέν ‘the possessions, for one’ answers to κουριδίην δ’ ἄλοχον ‘but the wedded wife’ at 392. ὅσ’ is ὅσα ‘as many as’, and ἠγάγετο the aorist middle of ἄγω, ‘brought with him’ (Paris said ἀγόμην of the same goods at 363). κοίλῃς ἐνὶ νηυσίν is the stock ‘in hollow ships’, with ἐνί for ἐν and the epic datives -ῃς and -σιν; Τροίηνδ’ is Τροίην with the suffix -δε ‘to’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 390.

sentences.t: ὡς πρὶν ὤφελλ’ ἀπολέσθαι·
sentences.tr: hōs prin ōphell’ apolesthai·
sentences.l: would that he had perished before!—
sentences.i: if only he had perished first!—
sentences.n: The herald’s own aside, breaking his sentence: he wishes Paris had died before he brought the goods and Helen home. ὡς … ὤφελλ’ is ὤφελλε, the epic doubled-λ form of ὤφειλε (ὀφείλω ‘ought’), which with ὡς and an infinitive makes a wish for what did not happen, ‘would that he had’, as ὤφελλον does at 6.350; ἀπολέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀπόλλυμαι ‘perish’, and πρίν ‘before’ means before the voyage. The subject is Alexander, carried over from the line before. The unit ends at the ano teleia that closes the line.

sentences.t: πάντ’ ἐθέλει δόμεναι καὶ οἴκοθεν ἄλλ’ ἐπιθεῖναι·
sentences.tr: pant’ ethelei domenai kai oikothen all’ epitheinai·
sentences.l: all he is willing to give, and to add others from his own house;
sentences.i: all these he is willing to give, and to add others from his own house besides;
sentences.n: The verb for the possessions of 389 at last: ἐθέλει δόμεναι ‘he is willing to give’, with πάντ’ (πάντα) ‘all’ taking up κτήματα, and δόμεναι the epic infinitive of δίδωμι. οἴκοθεν ἄλλ’ ἐπιθεῖναι is ‘to add other things from home’, with the suffix -θεν ‘from’ and ἐπιθεῖναι the aorist infinitive of ἐπιτίθημι ‘add’. The line is Paris’s own at 364, with ἐθέλει ‘he is willing’ for his ἐθέλω ‘I am willing’: the herald repeats the offer in Paris’s words, and the English follows the published line.

sentences.t:
κουριδίην δ’ ἄλοχον Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο
οὔ φησιν δώσειν·
sentences.tr:
kouridiēn d’ alochon Menelaou kydalimoio
ou phēsin dōsein·
sentences.l:
but the wedded wife of Menelaus the glorious,
he says he will not give;
sentences.i: but the wedded wife of glorious Menelaus he says he will not give;
sentences.n: The refusal, in substance what Paris said at 362 (γυναῖκα μὲν οὐκ ἀποδώσω), but Helen is now named by her marriage. κουριδίην ἄλοχον is ‘wedded wife’, κουρίδιος being the word for the lawful spouse of one’s youth; Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο ‘of glorious Menelaus’ has the epic genitive -οιο, and κυδάλιμος is his stock epithet, rendered as the table fixes it. οὔ φησιν δώσειν is ‘he says he will not give’: φησίν with the future infinitive of δίδωμι, the negative going in sense with the infinitive. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 393.

sentences.t: ἦ μὴν Τρῶές γε κέλονται.
sentences.tr: ē mēn Trōes ge kelontai.
sentences.l: truly, the Trojans at least urge him.
sentences.i: and yet the Trojans, for their part, are urging him to.
sentences.n: Idaeus adds on his own account that the Trojans want Helen given back, as Antenor proposed at 350. ἦ μήν is a strong asseveration, ‘truly indeed’, and γε singles out Τρῶες ‘the Trojans’ as against Paris. κέλονται is the present of κέλομαι ‘urge’; its object (Paris) and the thing urged (to give her) are both understood from the line before.

sentences.t:
καὶ δὲ τόδ’ ἠνώγεον εἰπεῖν ἔπος αἴ κ’ ἐθέλητε
παύσασθαι πολέμοιο δυσηχέος εἰς ὅ κε νεκροὺς
κήομεν· ὕστερον αὖτε μαχησόμεθ’ εἰς ὅ κε δαίμων
ἄμμε διακρίνῃ, δώῃ δ’ ἑτέροισί γε νίκην.
sentences.tr:
kai de tod’ ēnōgeon eipein epos ai k’ ethelēte
pausasthai polemoio dysēcheos eis ho ke nekrous
kēomen· hysteron aute machēsometh’ eis ho ke daimōn
amme diakrinēi, dōēi d’ heteroisi ge nikēn.
sentences.l:
And this too they bade me say, a word: whether you are willing
to cease from ill-sounding war, until the dead
we burn; later in turn we shall fight, until a divinity
parts us and gives victory to one side or the other.”
sentences.i: And they bade me say this too, a word: whether you are willing to cease from ill-sounding war until we burn the dead; later we shall fight again, until a divinity parts us and gives victory to one side or the other.”
sentences.n: The second message, the truce to burn the dead; lines 395–397 are Priam’s at 376–378 (and 396–397 Hector’s at 291–292), and keep their English. ἠνώγεον is the plural pluperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, now with all the Trojans as subject, and τόδ’ … ἔπος ‘this word’ looks ahead. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλητε ‘whether you are willing’ is addressed to the Achaeans, so the second person replaces Priam’s ἐθέλωσι; παύσασθαι takes the genitive πολέμοιο δυσηχέος ‘ill-sounding war’. εἰς ὅ κε … κήομεν is ‘until we burn’, and ἄμμε is ‘us’. The unit runs past the ano teleia in line 396, as the published unit at 375 does. Idaeus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ·
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent;
sentences.n: The Achaeans make no answer at first. The line is the stock one for a silence after a speech, and takes the English it has at 3.95. ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο with its vowel dropped and τ made θ before οἳ; οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες is ‘and they then all’. ἀκήν is an adverb, ‘hushed, still’, and σιωπῇ the dative of σιωπή ‘silence’ used adverbially; ἐγένοντο ‘became’ is the aorist of γίγνομαι. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: opse de dē meteeipe boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: But late indeed spoke among them Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: At last Diomedes, good at the war-cry, spoke among them:
sentences.n: Diomedes breaks the silence. The line is the introduction of a speaker who speaks late, in the pattern fixed for the Odyssey (20.321): ὀψὲ δὲ δή is ‘but late indeed’, after a pause, and μετέειπε ‘spoke among them’ (μετά ‘among’ with εἶπον). βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης ‘Diomedes, good at the war-cry’ is his stock title, βοήν being an accusative of respect, ‘good as to the shout’.

sentences.t:
μήτ’ ἄρ τις νῦν κτήματ’ Ἀλεξάνδροιο δεχέσθω
μήθ’ Ἑλένην·
sentences.tr:
mēt’ ar tis nyn ktēmat’ Alexandroio dechesthō
mēth’ Helenēn·
sentences.l:
“Let no one now, then, the possessions of Alexander accept,
nor Helen;
sentences.i: “Let no one now accept the possessions of Alexander, nor Helen;
sentences.n: Diomedes rejects both halves of the offer at once, the goods and Helen, though Helen was not offered. μήτ’ … μήθ’ is μήτε … μήτε ‘neither … nor’ (the second with θ before the rough breathing of Ἑλένην), with the third-person imperative δεχέσθω ‘let him accept’ (δέχομαι); τις is ‘anyone’, so the whole is ‘let no one accept’. ἄρ is the particle ἄρα ‘then’, drawing the conclusion from what Idaeus has said, and Ἀλεξάνδροιο is the epic genitive. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 401.

sentences.t:
γνωτὸν δὲ καὶ ὃς μάλα νήπιός ἐστιν
ὡς ἤδη Τρώεσσιν ὀλέθρου πείρατ’ ἐφῆπται.
sentences.tr:
gnōton de kai hos mala nēpios estin
hōs ēdē Trōessin olethrou peirat’ ephēptai.
sentences.l:
and it is known even to one who is very foolish
that already upon the Trojans the limits of destruction have been fastened.”
sentences.i: even a man who is very foolish knows that the limits of destruction have already been fastened upon the Trojans.”
sentences.n: His reason: the offer shows that the Trojans know they are losing. γνωτόν here is the neuter adjective ‘known’ (not the noun ‘kinsman’ of 3.174), with ἐστί understood, and καὶ ὃς μάλα νήπιός ἐστιν is ‘even one who is very foolish’. ὡς ‘that’ introduces what is known. ὀλέθρου πείρατ’ ἐφῆπται is the Odyssey’s phrase (22.41), ‘the limits of destruction have been fastened upon’: πείρατα is ‘ends, limits’, a word also used of rope-ends, so the picture may be of a cord bound round the Trojans; ἐφῆπται is the perfect passive of ἐφάπτω ‘fasten on’, singular with a neuter plural subject, and Τρώεσσιν the epic dative. Diomedes’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπίαχον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
μῦθον ἀγασσάμενοι Διομήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes epiachon huies Achaiōn
mython agassamenoi Diomēdeos hippodamoio·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all shouted, the sons of the Achaeans,
in admiration at the word of Diomedes, horse-taming;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all the sons of the Achaeans shouted in admiration at the word of Diomedes, tamer of horses;
sentences.n: The army approves with a shout. ἐπίαχον is an unaugmented aorist of ἐπιάχω ‘shout in response’ (ἰάχω ‘cry out’), and υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘the sons of the Achaeans’ stands in apposition to πάντες ‘all’. ἀγασσάμενοι is the aorist participle of ἄγαμαι, which means ‘wonder at, admire’ or ‘be indignant at’; at 7.41 the context asked for indignation, here the shout of assent asks for admiration, and the sense is chosen from the context. Διομήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο is ‘of Diomedes, tamer of horses’, his stock epithet. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ Ἰδαῖον προσέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: kai tot’ ar’ Idaion prosephē kreiōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: And then to Idaeus addressed lord Agamemnon:
sentences.i: And then lord Agamemnon said to Idaeus:
sentences.n: Agamemnon gives the herald the formal answer. The line is a speech-introduction of the kind built on τότε … προσέφη, ‘then he addressed’, used when the speaker is not replying to words said to him: καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and then, accordingly’, Ἰδαῖον the accusative object of προσέφη ‘addressed’ (πρόσφημι), and κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων ‘lord Agamemnon’ the stock title, κρείων meaning ‘ruler, lord’.

sentences.t:
Ἰδαῖ’ ἤτοι μῦθον Ἀχαιῶν αὐτὸς ἀκούεις
ὥς τοι ὑποκρίνονται·
sentences.tr:
Idai’ ētoi mython Achaiōn autos akoueis
hōs toi hypokrinontai·
sentences.l:
“Idaeus, truly the word of the Achaeans you yourself hear,
how they answer you;
sentences.i: “Idaeus, you yourself hear the word of the Achaeans, how they answer you;
sentences.n: Agamemnon lets the shout speak for the Achaeans. Ἰδαῖ’ is the vocative Ἰδαῖε elided; ἤτοι, printed as one word, is ‘truly’. μῦθον Ἀχαιῶν ‘the word of the Achaeans’ is their answer, and αὐτός ‘yourself’ stresses that Idaeus has heard it with his own ears. ὥς τοι ὑποκρίνονται is ‘how they answer you’: ὑποκρίνομαι is the Homeric verb for making a reply (Attic ἀποκρίνομαι), with τοι for σοι. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 407.

sentences.t:
ἐμοὶ δ’ ἐπιανδάνει οὕτως
ἀμφὶ δὲ νεκροῖσιν κατακαιέμεν οὔ τι μεγαίρω·
sentences.tr:
emoi d’ epiandanei houtōs
amphi de nekroisin katakaiemen ou ti megairō·
sentences.l:
and to me it is pleasing so;
and as for the dead, to burn them I do not at all grudge;
sentences.i: and so it pleases me too; and as for the dead, I do not at all grudge the burning of them;
sentences.n: Agamemnon adds his own voice to the refusal, then grants the truce. ἐπιανδάνει is the present of ἐπιανδάνω ‘please’, an epic compound of ἁνδάνω, with the dative ἐμοί; οὕτως ‘so’ is the answer the army has given. ἀμφὶ δὲ νεκροῖσιν is ‘and about the dead’, the preposition with the dative marking what the second clause concerns; κατακαιέμεν is the epic infinitive of κατακαίω ‘burn’, the object of μεγαίρω ‘grudge’ (the Odyssey’s word), with οὔ τι ‘not at all’. The edition prints no stop at the end of line 407; the δέ of the next line carries the sentence on, and the English supplies the pause.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τις φειδὼ νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων
γίγνετ’ ἐπεί κε θάνωσι πυρὸς μειλισσέμεν ὦκα.
sentences.tr:
ou gar tis pheidō nekyōn katatethnēōtōn
gignet’ epei ke thanōsi pyros meilissemen ōka.
sentences.l:
for there is no sparing of the dead, of those who have died,
once they have died, from appeasing them quickly with fire.
sentences.i: for when men have died, there is no holding back from giving the dead their due of fire without delay.
sentences.n: The reason the truce is granted: the dead must be burned, and that is owed to them. φειδώ is ‘sparing, holding back’, the noun of φείδομαι, and οὔ τις φειδὼ γίγνετ’ (γίγνεται) is ‘there comes to be no sparing’. νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων is the Odyssey’s phrase ‘of the dead, of those who have died’, with the perfect participle of καταθνῄσκω. ἐπεί κε θάνωσι is ‘once they have died’, κε with the subjunctive. μειλισσέμεν is the epic infinitive of μειλίσσω ‘soothe, appease’, here of appeasing the dead with their rites; πυρός ‘of fire’ is a partitive genitive, the fire being what the dead are given their share of, and ὦκα is ‘quickly’.

sentences.t: ὅρκια δὲ Ζεὺς ἴστω ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης.
sentences.tr: horkia de Zeus istō erigdoupos posis Hērēs.
sentences.l: and the oaths let Zeus know, the loud-crashing husband of Hera.”
sentences.i: and let Zeus, the loud-crashing husband of Hera, know of the oaths.”
sentences.n: Agamemnon calls Zeus to witness the truce. ὅρκια ‘oaths’ is the word for a sworn agreement and the things that seal it; ἴστω is the third-person imperative of οἶδα, ‘let him know’, and in an oath ‘know’ means ‘be witness to’, the sense the Odyssey’s ἴστω νῦν Ζεύς has at 14.158. ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης ‘loud-crashing husband of Hera’ is Zeus’s title in the Odyssey’s words: ἐρι- ‘loud’ with δοῦπος ‘a heavy crash’, thunder being only the traditional reading. Agamemnon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν τὸ σκῆπτρον ἀνέσχεθε πᾶσι θεοῖσιν,
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn to skēptron aneschethe pasi theoisin,
sentences.l: So having spoken, the sceptre he held up to all the gods,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and held up the sceptre to all the gods,
sentences.n: The gesture that goes with the oath. ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’, the aorist participle, and the subject is Agamemnon, who has just spoken; τὸ σκῆπτρον is the sceptre, the staff of a king, the article pointing at the one in his hand. ἀνέσχεθε is an aorist of ἀνέχω ‘hold up’ with the epic lengthened stem -σχεθ-, and πᾶσι θεοῖσιν ‘to all the gods’ has the epic dative in -σιν. Raising staff or hands to heaven marks an appeal to the gods, as when the people raised their hands at 7.177. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: ἄψορρον δ’ Ἰδαῖος ἔβη προτὶ Ἴλιον ἱρήν.
sentences.tr: apsorron d’ Idaios ebē proti Ilion hirēn.
sentences.l: and back again Idaeus went to sacred Ilium.
sentences.i: and Idaeus went back again to sacred Ilium.
sentences.n: The herald returns with the answer. ἄψορρον is an adverb, ‘back again’, built on ἄψ ‘back’; ἔβη is an unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘go’, and προτί the epic form of πρός ‘to, toward’. Ἴλιον ἱρήν ‘sacred Ilium’ is the city’s stock title, ἱρή being the epic form of ἱερή ‘sacred’; the Latin form ‘Ilium’ is kept for this phrase, as at 4.46.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἕατ’ εἰν ἀγορῇ Τρῶες καὶ Δαρδανίωνες
πάντες ὁμηγερέες, ποτιδέγμενοι ὁππότ’ ἄρ’ ἔλθοι
Ἰδαῖος·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ heat’ ein agorēi Trōes kai Dardaniōnes
pantes homēgerees, potidegmenoi hoppot’ ar’ elthoi
Idaios·
sentences.i: And they were sitting in assembly, Trojans and Dardanians, all gathered together, waiting for Idaeus to come;
sentences.n: The scene shifts to Troy, where the assembly waits for the herald. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ is explained by Τρῶες καὶ Δαρδανίωνες; Δαρδανίωνες is another form of Δάρδανοι ‘Dardanians’ (348), the people of Dardania in the Troad, kin to the Trojans. ἕατ’ is ἕατο, the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’; εἰν ἀγορῇ ‘in assembly’ has εἰν for ἐν. ὁμηγερέες is ‘gathered together’, and ποτιδέγμενοι (ποτί is πρός) a participle of προσδέχομαι ‘wait for’, with ὁππότ’ ἄρ’ ἔλθοι ‘when he should come’, an optative in past time for an awaited event; the name Ἰδαῖος is held back to the start of line 416. The unit ends at the ano teleia there.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἦλθε καὶ ἀγγελίην ἀπέειπε
στὰς ἐν μέσσοισιν·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ ēlthe kai angeliēn apeeipe
stas en messoisin·
sentences.l:
and he then came and the news delivered,
standing in their midst;
sentences.i: and he came and delivered his news, standing in their midst;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and he then’, the article as a pronoun; ἦλθε is the aorist of ἔρχομαι ‘come’. ἀγγελίην is ‘news’, the house word, here the Achaeans’ answer, and ἀπέειπε is the aorist of ἀπεῖπον in the sense ‘speak out, deliver’ (the same verb is ‘refuse’ at 1.515; the Odyssey has it of delivering a message at 16.340). στὰς ἐν μέσσοισιν ‘standing in their midst’ repeats the herald’s posture of 384. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 417.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ὁπλίζοντο μάλ’ ὦκα,
ἀμφότερον νέκυάς τ’ ἀγέμεν ἕτεροι δὲ μεθ’ ὕλην·
sentences.tr:
toi d’ hoplizonto mal’ ōka,
amphoteron nekyas t’ agemen heteroi de meth’ hylēn·
sentences.l:
and they made ready very quickly,
for both tasks: to bring the dead, and others to go for wood;
sentences.i: and they made ready very quickly for both tasks, some to bring the dead and others to fetch wood;
sentences.n: The Trojans divide the work. τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’, and ὁπλίζοντο the imperfect middle of ὁπλίζω ‘make ready’ (of arming or of any preparation); μάλ’ ὦκα is ‘very quickly’. ἀμφότερον is the neuter used as an adverb, ‘for both’, and what follows explains it: νέκυάς τ’ ἀγέμεν ‘to bring the dead’ (ἀγέμεν an epic infinitive of ἄγω; νέκυς is a corpse, νεκρός the other word used below) and ἕτεροι δὲ μεθ’ ὕλην ‘and others after wood’, μετά with the accusative meaning ‘in quest of’, with ‘go’ understood. The first party has no word of its own in the Greek; the plain layer supplies ‘some’.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐϋσσέλμων ἀπὸ νηῶν
ὀτρύνοντο νέκυς τ’ ἀγέμεν, ἕτεροι δὲ μεθ’ ὕλην.
sentences.tr:
Argeioi d’ heterōthen eÿsselmōn apo nēōn
otrynonto nekys t’ agemen, heteroi de meth’ hylēn.
sentences.l:
and the Argives on the other side, from the well-benched ships,
were urged on, to bring the dead, and others to go for wood.
sentences.i: and the Argives on the other side, from the well-benched ships, were urged on, some to bring the dead and others to fetch wood.
sentences.n: The Achaean side does the same, in nearly the same words. ἑτέρωθεν is ‘from the other side’, and ἐϋσσέλμων ἀπὸ νηῶν ‘from the well-benched ships’, with the stock epithet (ἐΰ ‘well’ with σέλμα ‘rowing-bench’) and the epic genitive plural νηῶν. ὀτρύνοντο is the imperfect middle or passive of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, ‘were urged on, bestirred themselves’. νέκυς here is the accusative plural, an epic form beside νέκυας in 418, and the half-line ἀγέμεν ἕτεροι δὲ μεθ’ ὕλην repeats 418 and keeps its English.

sentences.t:
Ἠέλιος μὲν ἔπειτα νέον προσέβαλλεν ἀρούρας
ἐξ ἀκαλαρρείταο βαθυρρόου Ὠκεανοῖο
οὐρανὸν εἰσανιών·
sentences.tr:
Ēelios men epeita neon proseballen arouras
ex akalarreitao bathyrroou Ōkeanoio
ouranon eisaniōn·
sentences.i: The Sun was just then striking the fields, out of gently flowing, deep-flowing Oceanus, as he climbed into heaven;
sentences.n: Sunrise, in the Odyssey’s words (19.433–434), which keep their English. Ἠέλιος is the Sun; μὲν ἔπειτα ‘then’, and νέον ‘newly, just now’ an adverb. προσέβαλλεν is the imperfect of προσβάλλω ‘strike against’, with ἀρούρας ‘the fields’ (ἄρουρα, ploughed land). ἐξ … Ὠκεανοῖο is ‘out of Oceanus’, the river that rings the earth and from which the Sun rises, with the epic genitives ἀκαλαρρείταο ‘gently-flowing’ (ἀκαλός ‘quiet’ with the root of ῥέω) and βαθυρρόου ‘deep-flowing’. εἰσανιών is the participle of εἰσάνειμι ‘go up into’, with οὐρανόν ‘heaven’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 423.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ἤντεον ἀλλήλοισιν.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ēnteon allēloisin.
sentences.l: and they met one another.
sentences.i: and the two sides met one another.
sentences.n: The two parties come together on the battlefield to gather their dead. οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ takes in both sides; ἤντεον is the imperfect of ἀντάω ‘meet’, uncontracted (Attic ἤντων), and takes the dative ἀλλήλοισιν ‘one another’.

sentences.t: ἔνθα διαγνῶναι χαλεπῶς ἦν ἄνδρα ἕκαστον·
sentences.tr: entha diagnōnai chalepōs ēn andra hekaston·
sentences.l: There to tell apart each man was hard;
sentences.i: There it was hard to tell each man apart;
sentences.n: The bodies were hard to recognise. ἔνθα is ‘there’; διαγνῶναι is the aorist infinitive of διαγιγνώσκω ‘distinguish, tell apart’, with ἄνδρα ἕκαστον ‘each man’ as its object; χαλεπῶς ἦν is ‘it was with difficulty’, the adverb with ‘was’ standing for ‘it was hard’. The next lines give the reason: the dead were covered in gore.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὕδατι νίζοντες ἄπο βρότον αἱματόεντα
δάκρυα θερμὰ χέοντες ἀμαξάων ἐπάειραν.
sentences.tr:
all’ hydati nizontes apo broton haimatoenta
dakrya therma cheontes amaxaōn epaeiran.
sentences.l:
but with water washing off the bloody gore,
shedding hot tears, they lifted them onto the wagons.
sentences.i: but they washed off the bloody gore with water and, shedding hot tears, lifted them onto the wagons.
sentences.n: The dead are washed and loaded. ἀλλ’ answers the difficulty of 424: the faces could be known only once washed. νίζοντες … ἄπο is a split compound, ἀπονίζω ‘wash off’, with the preverb after its verb and accented ἄπο; ὕδατι is ‘with water’, and βρότον αἱματόεντα ‘bloody gore’ (βρότος is clotted blood, a different word from βροτός ‘mortal’). δάκρυα θερμὰ χέοντες is ‘shedding hot tears’. ἐπάειραν is the aorist of ἐπαείρω ‘lift onto’, with the genitive ἀμαξάων ‘the wagons’, the epic genitive plural of ἄμαξα; the object, the dead, is understood.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ εἴα κλαίειν Πρίαμος μέγας·
sentences.tr: oud’ eia klaiein Priamos megas·
sentences.l: Nor did great Priam allow them to weep;
sentences.i: Nor did great Priam allow them to weep;
sentences.n: Priam forbids open mourning. εἴα is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, with οὐδ’ ‘nor’; κλαίειν is ‘to weep, wail’, the loud lament for the dead, and the object ‘them’ is understood. Πρίαμος μέγας is ‘great Priam’, the adjective at the end of its phrase. The Greek gives no reason for the order; the tears of 426 show the grief was there. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ σιωπῇ
νεκροὺς πυρκαϊῆς ἐπινήνεον ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ,
ἐν δὲ πυρὶ πρήσαντες ἔβαν προτὶ Ἴλιον ἱρήν.
sentences.tr:
hoi de siōpēi
nekrous pyrkaïēs epinēneon achnymenoi kēr,
en de pyri prēsantes eban proti Ilion hirēn.
sentences.l:
and they in silence
the dead upon the pyre heaped up, grieving in heart,
and having burned them in the fire went to sacred Ilium.
sentences.i: and they heaped the dead upon the pyre in silence, grieving in heart, and when they had burned them in the fire they went to sacred Ilium.
sentences.n: The Trojan burning. οἳ δέ ‘and they’; σιωπῇ ‘in silence’, as Priam ordered. νεκρούς ‘the dead’ (νεκρός, beside νέκυς above) is the object of ἐπινήνεον, an imperfect of ἐπινηνέω ‘heap upon’, with the genitive πυρκαϊῆς ‘the pyre’ (πυρκαϊή, the burning-place, from πῦρ). ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ is ‘grieving in heart’, κῆρ an accusative of respect. ἐν δὲ πυρὶ πρήσαντες is ‘having burned them in the fire’, the aorist participle of πρήθω ‘burn’; ἔβαν is the epic third-person plural aorist of βαίνω, ‘went’, and προτὶ Ἴλιον ἱρήν ‘to sacred Ilium’ as at 413. Line 428 returns at 431 and keeps its English there.

sentences.t:
ὣς δ’ αὔτως ἑτέρωθεν ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
νεκροὺς πυρκαϊῆς ἐπινήνεον ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ,
ἐν δὲ πυρὶ πρήσαντες ἔβαν κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας.
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ autōs heterōthen eÿknēmides Achaioi
nekrous pyrkaïēs epinēneon achnymenoi kēr,
en de pyri prēsantes eban koilas epi nēas.
sentences.l:
And just so, on the other side, the well-greaved Achaeans
the dead upon the pyre heaped up, grieving in heart,
and having burned them in the fire went to the hollow ships.
sentences.i: And in just the same way, on the other side, the well-greaved Achaeans heaped the dead upon the pyre, grieving in heart, and when they had burned them in the fire they went to the hollow ships.
sentences.n: The Achaean burning, in the same words as the Trojan one, with the ships in place of the city. ὣς δ’ αὔτως is ‘and just so’, the house rendering; ἑτέρωθεν ‘on the other side’; ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί ‘well-greaved Achaeans’ is the stock epithet (κνημίς ‘greave’, the shin-guard). Line 431 is line 428 again, and the first half of 432 is that of 429; both keep their English. κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας is ‘to the hollow ships’, as at 381. The poet gives the two sides one grief and one rite.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ οὔτ’ ἄρ πω ἠώς, ἔτι δ’ ἀμφιλύκη νύξ,
τῆμος ἄρ’ ἀμφὶ πυρὴν κριτὸς ἔγρετο λαὸς Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.tr:
ēmos d’ out’ ar pō ēōs, eti d’ amphilykē nyx,
tēmos ar’ amphi pyrēn kritos egreto laos Achaiōn,
sentences.l:
And when it was not yet dawn, but still the twilight of night,
then around the pyre a chosen people of the Achaeans awoke,
sentences.i: And when it was not yet dawn, but still the twilight of night, a chosen body of the Achaean army awoke around the pyre,
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the Achaean wall is built before daybreak. ἦμος … τῆμος is ‘when … then’; οὔτ’ ἄρ πω ἠώς is ‘it was not yet dawn’ (ἦν understood), and ἀμφιλύκη, of the night, is a word found only here: it is usually explained from λύκη ‘light’ (the root of λυκάβας and Latin lux), ‘with light about it’, twilight, and that traditional reading is given. κριτός is ‘chosen, picked’; λαός is ‘people’ in the literal layer and ‘army’ in the plain, as the house keeps it. ἔγρετο is an aorist middle of ἐγείρω, ‘awoke’. The sentence runs on, cut at the comma because it would otherwise fill five lines.

sentences.t:
τύμβον δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτὴν ἕνα ποίεον ἐξαγαγόντες
ἄκριτον ἐκ πεδίου, ποτὶ δ’ αὐτὸν τεῖχος ἔδειμαν
πύργους θ’ ὑψηλούς, εἶλαρ νηῶν τε καὶ αὐτῶν.
sentences.tr:
tymbon d’ amph’ autēn hena poieon exagagontes
akriton ek pediou, poti d’ auton teichos edeiman
pyrgous th’ hypsēlous, eilar nēōn te kai autōn.
sentences.l:
and a mound around it, one, they made, leading out,
unsorted, from the plain, and against it a wall they built
and high towers, a shelter for the ships and for themselves.
sentences.i: and they brought the dead out of the plain and made around the pyre one undivided mound, and against it they built a wall and high towers, a shelter for the ships and for themselves.
sentences.n: Nestor’s plan of 336–338 is carried out, in his own words with the verbs made past: ποίεον ‘they made’ (unaugmented imperfect of ποιέω) for his χεύομεν, ἔδειμαν ‘they built’ (aorist of δέμω) for δείμομεν. τύμβον … ἕνα … ἄκριτον is ‘one mound, unsorted’: ἄκριτος keeps ‘unsorted’ in the literal layer and the sense ‘undivided’, one mound for all, in the plain, as at 337; ἀμφ’ αὐτήν ‘around it’ is the pyre. ἐξαγαγόντες ἐκ πεδίου ‘having led out of the plain’ has the dead understood. ποτὶ δ’ αὐτόν ‘and against it’, the mound, adds τεῖχος ‘a wall’, which Nestor had not named, to πύργους ὑψηλούς ‘high towers’.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ αὐτοῖσι πύλας ἐνεποίεον εὖ ἀραρυίας,
ὄφρα δι’ αὐτάων ἱππηλασίη ὁδὸς εἴη·
sentences.tr:
en d’ autoisi pylas enepoieon eu araruias,
ophra di’ autaōn hippēlasiē hodos eiē·
sentences.l:
and in them gates they made, well fitted,
so that through them a horse-driving road might be;
sentences.i: and they made well-fitted gates in them, so that there might be a road for driving horses through them;
sentences.n: The gates, again in Nestor’s words (339–340), with ἐνεποίεον ‘they made in’ (unaugmented imperfect of ἐμποιέω) for his ποιήσομεν ‘let us make’; line 439 is his line unchanged and keeps its English, with ‘might’ for ‘may’ because the purpose clause now follows a past tense. ἐν δ’ αὐτοῖσι is ‘and in them’, the towers and wall; ἀραρυίας is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, feminine accusative plural with πύλας ‘gates’. δι’ αὐτάων ‘through them’ is the epic genitive plural, and ἱππηλασίη ὁδός ‘a road for driving horses’ (ἵππος with ἐλαύνω); εἴη is the optative of εἰμί.

sentences.t:
ἔκτοσθεν δὲ βαθεῖαν ἐπ’ αὐτῷ τάφρον ὄρυξαν
εὐρεῖαν μεγάλην, ἐν δὲ σκόλοπας κατέπηξαν.
sentences.tr:
ektosthen de batheian ep’ autōi taphron oryxan
eureian megalēn, en de skolopas katepēxan.
sentences.l:
and outside, a deep ditch close by it they dug,
wide and great, and in it stakes they fixed.
sentences.i: and outside, close by the wall, they dug a deep ditch, wide and great, and fixed stakes in it.
sentences.n: The ditch, Nestor’s last item (341), with ὄρυξαν ‘they dug’ (aorist of ὀρύσσω) for his ὀρύξομεν; the stakes are new. ἔκτοσθεν is ‘outside’, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘close by it’, the wall, ἐπί with the dative of nearness. τάφρον ‘ditch’ has three adjectives, βαθεῖαν ‘deep’, εὐρεῖαν ‘wide’, μεγάλην ‘great’. ἐν δέ ‘and in it’ is the preposition used as an adverb; σκόλοπες are ‘stakes’, pointed timbers, and κατέπηξαν the aorist of καταπήγνυμι ‘fix firmly, plant’.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν πονέοντο κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.tr: hōs hoi men poneonto karē komoōntes Achaioi·
sentences.l: So they, for their part, were toiling, the long-haired-of-head Achaeans;
sentences.i: So the long-haired Achaeans toiled;
sentences.n: The scene turns from the men to the gods watching them. ὣς οἳ μέν ‘so they, for their part’ is answered by οἳ δὲ θεοί ‘but the gods’ in the next line; πονέοντο is the uncontracted imperfect of πονέομαι ‘toil’. κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί ‘the long-haired-of-head Achaeans’ is the stock phrase, κάρη ‘head’ an accusative of respect with κομόωντες ‘wearing long hair’ (κομάω, with the epic doubled vowel). A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ θεοὶ πὰρ Ζηνὶ καθήμενοι ἀστεροπητῇ
θηεῦντο μέγα ἔργον Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων.
sentences.tr:
hoi de theoi par Zēni kathēmenoi asteropētēi
thēeunto mega ergon Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn.
sentences.l:
and the gods, beside Zeus the lightning-flasher seated,
were marvelling at the great work of the bronze-shirted Achaeans.
sentences.i: and the gods, seated beside Zeus who flashes lightning, gazed in wonder at the great work of the bronze-shirted Achaeans.
sentences.n: The gods look on. οἳ δὲ θεοὶ πὰρ Ζηνὶ καθήμενοι ‘the gods, seated beside Zeus’ opens as 4.1 does; Ζηνί is the epic dative of Ζεύς, and ἀστεροπητῇ ‘the lightning-flasher’ (from ἀστεροπή ‘lightning’) agrees with it, the epithet at the end of the line. θηεῦντο is the imperfect of θηέομαι ‘gaze at, marvel at’ (Attic θεάομαι), rendered as the Odyssey renders it. μέγα ἔργον is ‘the great work’, the wall, and Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων ‘of the bronze-shirted Achaeans’ the stock epithet (χαλκός with χιτών).

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.tr: toisi de mythōn ērche Poseidaōn enosichthōn·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning Poseidon earth-shaker:
sentences.i: Poseidon earth-shaker was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: Poseidon opens the talk. The line is the stock introduction of the first speaker in a company, in the house pattern (Odyssey 3.417): τοῖσι ‘among them’, μύθων ἦρχε ‘began the speeches’ (ἄρχω with the genitive, ‘make a beginning of’). Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων is ‘Poseidon earth-shaker’, the god’s stock title, the epithet joining a root meaning ‘shake’ to χθών ‘earth’.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἦ ῥά τίς ἐστι βροτῶν ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν
ὅς τις ἔτ’ ἀθανάτοισι νόον καὶ μῆτιν ἐνίψει;
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater, ē rha tis esti brotōn ep’ apeirona gaian
hos tis et’ athanatoisi noon kai mētin enipsei;
sentences.l:
“Zeus father, is there then anyone of mortals over the boundless earth
who will still to the immortals his mind and his cunning declare?
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, is there any mortal now on the boundless earth who will still declare his mind and his cunning to the immortals?
sentences.n: Poseidon’s complaint: men have stopped telling the gods their plans. Ζεῦ πάτερ is the vocative ‘Father Zeus’. ἦ ῥά τίς ἐστι is a question, ‘is there then anyone’, ἦ interrogative and ῥα ‘then’; βροτῶν ‘of mortals’ is partitive, and ἐπ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν ‘over the boundless earth’ the Odyssey’s phrase. ὅς τις … ἐνίψει is ‘who will declare’: ἐνίψει is taken as the future of ἐνέπω ‘tell’ (the form has also been referred to ἐνίπτω ‘rebuke’, which does not suit the sense), and νόον καὶ μῆτιν ‘mind and cunning’ are a man’s thought and the plan he forms from it; ἔτ’ is ἔτι ‘still, any more’. Poseidon’s speech begins.

sentences.l:
Do you not see that now in turn the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
a wall have built as a wall above the ships, and around it a ditch
have driven, and to the gods have not given famous hecatombs?
sentences.i: Do you not see that the long-haired Achaeans have now built a wall to shield the ships, and driven a ditch around it, and have not given the gods famous hecatombs?
sentences.n: The grievance made plain. ὁράᾳς is ‘you see’, ὁράω with the epic doubled vowel; ὅτι δ’ αὖτε is ‘that now in turn’, δέ standing oddly inside the ὅτι clause. τεῖχος ἐτειχίσσαντο is ‘they have built themselves a wall’, the verb τειχίζω made from the noun, so the literal layer keeps both. νεῶν ὕπερ is ‘above the ships’, ὕπερ after its noun: the wall stands landward of the beached ships, to protect them, and the plain layer gives that sense. ἀμφὶ … τάφρον ἤλασαν is ‘drove a ditch around’. κλειτὰς ἑκατόμβας is ‘famous hecatombs’ (κλειτός is κλυτός ‘famous’), a hecatomb being properly a hundred oxen; δόσαν is an unaugmented aorist, ‘gave’.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ ἤτοι κλέος ἔσται ὅσον τ’ ἐπικίδναται ἠώς·
sentences.tr: tou d’ ētoi kleos estai hoson t’ epikidnatai ēōs·
sentences.l: Of this, truly, the fame will be as far as the dawn spreads;
sentences.i: The fame of this will truly reach as far as the dawn spreads;
sentences.n: The new wall will be famous, and the gods’ own wall forgotten. τοῦ ‘of this’ is the article as a demonstrative, the wall just described; ἤτοι ‘truly’; κλέος ἔσται ‘fame will be’. ὅσον τ’ ἐπικίδναται ἠώς is ‘as far as the dawn spreads’, that is, over the whole earth: ἐπικίδναμαι ‘spread over’, with the epic τε of a general truth, and ἠώς ‘dawn’ for daylight. Zeus turns this very line back on Poseidon at 458.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἐπιλήσονται τὸ ἐγὼ καὶ Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
ἥρῳ Λαομέδοντι πολίσσαμεν ἀθλήσαντε.
sentences.tr:
tou d’ epilēsontai to egō kai Phoibos Apollōn
hērōi Laomedonti polissamen athlēsante.
sentences.l:
but that they will forget, which I and Phoebus Apollo
for the hero Laomedon built as a city, the two of us having laboured.”
sentences.i: but they will forget the wall that I and Phoebus Apollo built as a city for the hero Laomedon, the two of us toiling at it.”
sentences.n: The gods’ own wall at Troy. τοῦ δ’ ἐπιλήσονται is ‘but that they will forget’, ἐπιλανθάνομαι taking the genitive; τό ‘which’ is the article as a relative, picking up the wall. ἥρῳ Λαομέδοντι is ‘for the hero Laomedon’, a king of Troy before Priam (the same Laomedon as at 5.269 and 6.23); ἥρως takes the house ‘the hero’. πολίσσαμεν is the aorist of πολίζω ‘build as a city, wall’, and ἀθλήσαντε the dual aorist participle of ἀθλέω ‘toil, labour’, for the two gods. Poseidon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: ton de meg’ ochthēsas prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Him, greatly vexed, addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: Greatly troubled, Zeus who gathers the clouds said to him:
sentences.n: Zeus answers, with the masculine form of the speech-introduction used of Thetis and Hera at 1.517 and 4.30: τόν ‘him’ is Poseidon, μέγ’ ὀχθήσας ‘greatly vexed’ the aorist participle of ὀχθέω, a mood of annoyance, and προσέφη ‘addressed’. νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς is ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’ (νεφέλη ‘cloud’ with ἀγείρω ‘gather’), a nominative in -α. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι ἐννοσίγαι’ εὐρυσθενές, οἷον ἔειπες.
sentences.tr: ō popoi ennosigai’ eurysthenes, hoion eeipes.
sentences.l: “Ah, earth-shaker, of wide strength, what a thing you have said.
sentences.i: “Ah, earth-shaker, of far-reaching strength, what a thing you have said.
sentences.n: Zeus’s opening is the line he speaks to Poseidon in the Odyssey (13.140), and keeps its English. ὢ πόποι is a cry of surprise or displeasure, ‘Ah’; ἐννοσίγαι’ is the vocative ἐννοσίγαιε ‘earth-shaker’ elided, a compound built on γαῖα as ἐνοσίχθων is on χθών, and εὐρυσθενές the vocative of εὐρυσθενής ‘of wide strength’ (εὐρύς with σθένος). οἷον ἔειπες is ‘what a thing you have said’, ἔειπες the epic aorist of εἶπον with the doubled vowel. Zeus’s speech begins.

sentences.t:
ἄλλός κέν τις τοῦτο θεῶν δείσειε νόημα,
ὃς σέο πολλὸν ἀφαυρότερος χεῖράς τε μένος τε·
sentences.tr:
allos ken tis touto theōn deiseie noēma,
hos seo pollon aphauroteros cheiras te menos te·
sentences.l:
Another of the gods might fear this thought,
one who is far weaker than you in hands and in might;
sentences.i: Some other god might fear this thought, one far weaker than you in his hands and his might;
sentences.n: Zeus says the fear is beneath Poseidon. ἄλλός … τις θεῶν is ‘some other one of the gods’; κέν … δείσειε is a potential optative, ‘might fear’, aorist of δείδω; τοῦτο … νόημα ‘this thought’ is the Achaeans’ plan, or the thought that the gods are being forgotten. ὅς ‘one who’ has ἐστί understood; σέο is the epic genitive ‘than you’ after the comparative ἀφαυρότερος ‘weaker’ (ἀφαυρός ‘weak’), with πολλόν ‘by far’ an adverb, and χεῖράς τε μένος τε ‘in hands and might’ accusatives of respect.

sentences.t: σὸν δ’ ἤτοι κλέος ἔσται ὅσον τ’ ἐπικίδναται ἠώς.
sentences.tr: son d’ ētoi kleos estai hoson t’ epikidnatai ēōs.
sentences.l: but your fame, truly, will be as far as the dawn spreads.
sentences.i: Your fame, truly, will reach as far as the dawn spreads.
sentences.n: Zeus gives Poseidon back his own words of 451, with σόν ‘your’ in place of τοῦ ‘of this’: it is the god’s fame, not the wall’s, that will cover the earth. ἤτοι is ‘truly’, κλέος ‘fame’, and ὅσον τ’ ἐπικίδναται ἠώς ‘as far as the dawn spreads’ as before, the shared words keeping the same English.

sentences.t:
ἄγρει μὰν ὅτ’ ἂν αὖτε κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
οἴχωνται σὺν νηυσὶ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
τεῖχος ἀναρρήξας τὸ μὲν εἰς ἅλα πᾶν καταχεῦαι,
sentences.tr:
agrei man hot’ an aute karē komoōntes Achaioi
oichōntai syn nēusi philēn es patrida gaian
teichos anarrēxas to men eis hala pan katacheuai,
sentences.l:
Come then, when in turn the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
have gone with their ships to their dear fatherland,
the wall break up and pour it all into the salt-sea,
sentences.i: Come then, when the long-haired Achaeans have gone back with their ships to their dear fatherland, break up the wall and pour the whole of it into the sea,
sentences.n: Zeus’s remedy: wait, then wipe the wall out. ἄγρει μάν is ‘come then’, an old imperative used as an interjection, with μάν (Attic μήν) ‘indeed’. ὅτ’ ἂν … οἴχωνται is ‘whenever they have gone’, subjunctive with ἄν; φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘to their dear fatherland’ is the stock close, with ἐς for εἰς. ἀναρρήξας is the aorist participle of ἀναρρήγνυμι ‘break up’, and καταχεῦαι the aorist infinitive of καταχέω ‘pour down’, used as an imperative; τὸ μὲν … πᾶν ‘all of it’ is the wall, and εἰς ἅλα ‘into the salt-sea’ (ἅλς). The sentence is cut at the comma, since it would otherwise fill five lines.

sentences.t:
αὖτις δ’ ἠϊόνα μεγάλην ψαμάθοισι καλύψαι,
ὥς κέν τοι μέγα τεῖχος ἀμαλδύνηται Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
autis d’ ēïona megalēn psamathoisi kalypsai,
hōs ken toi mega teichos amaldynētai Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
and again the great beach with sands cover over,
so that for you the great wall of the Achaeans may be made to vanish.”
sentences.i: and cover the great beach over again with sands, so that the great wall of the Achaeans may be wiped out for you.”
sentences.n: The second command and its purpose. αὖτις is ‘again’, ἠϊόνα μεγάλην ‘the great beach’ (ἠϊών, the shore), and ψαμάθοισι καλύψαι ‘cover with sands’, another infinitive as imperative, with the dative plural of ψάμαθος ‘sand’ as in the published parts. ὥς κέν … ἀμαλδύνηται is a purpose clause with κε and the subjunctive: ἀμαλδύνω is ‘efface, make to disappear’, here passive, and τοι ‘for you’ is σοι. μέγα τεῖχος … Ἀχαιῶν ‘the great wall of the Achaeans’ is the ἔργον of 444. Zeus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
δύσετο δ’ ἠέλιος, τετέλεστο δὲ ἔργον Ἀχαιῶν,
βουφόνεον δὲ κατὰ κλισίας καὶ δόρπον ἕλοντο.
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon,
dyseto d’ ēelios, tetelesto de ergon Achaiōn,
bouphoneon de kata klisias kai dorpon helonto.
sentences.l:
So they, on the one hand, such things to one another were speaking,
and the sun set, and the work of the Achaeans was completed,
and they slaughtered oxen among the huts and took their supper.
sentences.i: So they spoke such words to one another, and the sun set, and the work of the Achaeans was completed, and they slaughtered oxen among the huts and took their supper.
sentences.n: Back to earth: evening and the meal. The first line is the stock close to a conversation (as at 5.274) and keeps its English; ἀγόρευον is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω. δύσετο is a mixed aorist of δύω ‘set’, with ἠέλιος ‘the sun’; τετέλεστο is the pluperfect passive of τελέω, ‘had been completed’, given as a simple past, the house ‘fulfil’ being kept for plans and promises, where ἔργον ‘work’ asks for ‘completed’. βουφόνεον is the imperfect of βουφονέω ‘slaughter oxen’ (βοῦς with φόνος), κατὰ κλισίας ‘among the huts’, and δόρπον ἕλοντο ‘took their supper’, as the Trojans did at 380. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
νῆες δ’ ἐκ Λήμνοιο παρέσταν οἶνον ἄγουσαι
πολλαί, τὰς προέηκεν Ἰησονίδης Εὔνηος,
τόν ῥ’ ἔτεχ’ Ὑψιπύλη ὑπ’ Ἰήσονι ποιμένι λαῶν.
sentences.tr:
nēes d’ ek Lēmnoio parestan oinon agousai
pollai, tas proeēken Iēsonidēs Eunēos,
ton rh’ etech’ Hypsipylē hyp’ Iēsoni poimeni laōn.
sentences.l:
And ships from Lemnos came alongside, bringing wine,
many of them, which Jason’s-son Euneus had sent forth,
whom Hypsipyle bore to Jason, shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: And ships from Lemnos came in, many of them, bringing wine, sent by Euneus the son of Jason, whom Hypsipyle had borne to Jason, shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: Supplies arrive from the island of Lemnos. παρέσταν is the epic third-person plural aorist of παρίστημι, ‘stood beside, came alongside’, and ἄγουσαι ‘bringing’ the participle agreeing with νῆες; πολλαί ‘many’ is held to the next line. προέηκεν is the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forth’. Ἰησονίδης is ‘Jason’s son’, the patronymic hyphenated in the literal layer like Ἀτρεΐδης, and Εὔνηος the son’s name; ἔτεχ’ is ἔτεκε ‘bore’ (τίκτω), and ὑπ’ Ἰήσονι ‘under Jason’ names the father, the poem’s way of saying to whom a mother bore her child; ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is the stock title of a leader. Jason is Ἰήσων here, with the Ionic η.

sentences.t:
χωρὶς δ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃς Ἀγαμέμνονι καὶ Μενελάῳ
δῶκεν Ἰησονίδης ἀγέμεν μέθυ χίλια μέτρα.
sentences.tr:
chōris d’ Atreïdēis Agamemnoni kai Menelaōi
dōken Iēsonidēs agemen methy chilia metra.
sentences.l:
and separately, to the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus,
Jason’s-son gave wine to carry off, a thousand measures.
sentences.i: and separately Jason’s son gave the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus, a thousand measures of wine to carry off.
sentences.n: A gift for the two kings apart from the cargo for sale. χωρίς is ‘separately, apart’; Ἀτρεΐδῃς Ἀγαμέμνονι καὶ Μενελάῳ ‘to the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus’ repeats 373 and keeps its English, with the dative plural in -ῃς. δῶκεν ‘gave’ is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι, and ἀγέμεν the epic infinitive of ἄγω, ‘to carry off’. μέθυ is ‘wine’ (the Odyssey’s μέθυ ἡδύ is ‘sweet wine’), and χίλια μέτρα ‘a thousand measures’, the measure being a vessel of fixed size that the Greek does not define.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν οἰνίζοντο κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί,
ἄλλοι μὲν χαλκῷ, ἄλλοι δ’ αἴθωνι σιδήρῳ,
ἄλλοι δὲ ῥινοῖς, ἄλλοι δ’ αὐτῇσι βόεσσιν,
ἄλλοι δ’ ἀνδραπόδεσσι·
sentences.tr:
enthen oinizonto karē komoōntes Achaioi,
alloi men chalkōi, alloi d’ aithōni sidērōi,
alloi de rhinois, alloi d’ autēisi boessin,
alloi d’ andrapodessi·
sentences.l:
From there the long-haired-of-head Achaeans got themselves wine,
some with bronze, some with fire-bright iron,
some with hides, some with the oxen themselves,
some with slaves;
sentences.i: From there the long-haired Achaeans got themselves wine, some paying with bronze, some with fire-bright iron, some with hides, some with the oxen themselves, and some with slaves;
sentences.n: Barter for the wine, five goods named. ἔνθεν is ‘from there’, from the ships; οἰνίζοντο is the imperfect middle of οἰνίζομαι ‘get wine for oneself’, a verb made from οἶνος. ἄλλοι μέν … ἄλλοι δέ ‘some … others’, each with a dative of price: χαλκῷ ‘bronze’, αἴθωνι σιδήρῳ ‘fire-bright iron’ (the house phrase, the colour of iron in the fire), ῥινοῖς ‘hides’, αὐτῇσι βόεσσιν ‘the oxen themselves’, live beasts as against their hides, with the epic datives -ῃσι and -εσσι, and ἀνδραπόδεσσι ‘slaves’, ἀνδράποδον being a captive held as property, a word found only here in Homer. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 475.

sentences.t: τίθεντο δὲ δαῖτα θάλειαν.
sentences.tr: tithento de daita thaleian.
sentences.l: and they made ready an abundant feast.
sentences.i: and they made ready an abundant feast.
sentences.n: τίθεντο is the imperfect middle of τίθημι, here ‘set out for themselves, made ready’; δαῖτα θάλειαν is ‘an abundant feast’, the stock phrase (θάλεια from the root of θάλλω ‘flourish’), kept to the house rendering. The unit ends at the full stop that closes the line.

sentences.t:
παννύχιοι μὲν ἔπειτα κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοὶ
δαίνυντο, Τρῶες δὲ κατὰ πτόλιν ἠδ’ ἐπίκουροι·
sentences.tr:
pannychioi men epeita karē komoōntes Achaioi
dainynto, Trōes de kata ptolin ēd’ epikouroi·
sentences.l:
All night long then the long-haired-of-head Achaeans
feasted, and the Trojans throughout the city, and the allies;
sentences.i: Then all night long the long-haired Achaeans feasted, and so did the Trojans throughout the city, and their allies;
sentences.n: Both sides feast; the next lines set Zeus against them. παννύχιοι is an adjective used as an adverb, ‘all night long’ (πᾶς with νύξ), agreeing with Ἀχαιοί; μέν is answered by Τρῶες δέ. δαίνυντο is the imperfect of δαίνυμαι ‘feast’, understood again for the Trojans. κατὰ πτόλιν ‘throughout the city’ has the epic πτόλις for πόλις, and ἠδ’ ἐπίκουροι ‘and the allies’ are the fighters from elsewhere who help Troy.

sentences.t:
παννύχιος δέ σφιν κακὰ μήδετο μητίετα Ζεὺς
σμερδαλέα κτυπέων·
sentences.tr:
pannychios de sphin kaka mēdeto mētieta Zeus
smerdalea ktypeōn·
sentences.l:
and all night long for them evils was devising counsellor Zeus,
terribly thundering;
sentences.i: and all night long Zeus the counsellor was devising evils for them, thundering terribly;
sentences.n: The thunder is an omen of harm to come. παννύχιος is now singular, of Zeus; σφιν ‘for them’ is both armies. κακὰ μήδετο ‘was devising evils’ is the Odyssey’s phrase (14.243), with μήδομαι ‘devise’; μητίετα Ζεύς ‘counsellor Zeus’ is his stock title, from μῆτις, and the English keeps it even where the counsellor plans harm. σμερδαλέα is the neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘terribly’, and κτυπέων the participle of κτυπέω ‘crash, thunder’ (κτύπος ‘crash’). The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 479.

sentences.t: τοὺς δὲ χλωρὸν δέος ᾕρει·
sentences.tr: tous de chlōron deos hēirei·
sentences.l: and them pale fear was seizing;
sentences.i: and pale fear seized them;
sentences.n: The half-line is the Odyssey’s (12.243) and keeps its English. τούς ‘them’ is the article as a pronoun; χλωρὸν δέος is ‘pale fear’, χλωρός being the green-yellow of young growth and of a face drained of blood; ᾕρει is the imperfect of αἱρέω ‘seize, take hold of’, the fear coming over them as the thunder went on. The unit ends at the ano teleia that closes the line.

sentences.t:
οἶνον δ’ ἐκ δεπάων χαμάδις χέον, οὐδέ τις ἔτλη
πρὶν πιέειν πρὶν λεῖψαι ὑπερμενέϊ Κρονίωνι.
sentences.tr:
oinon d’ ek depaōn chamadis cheon, oude tis etlē
prin pieein prin leipsai hypermeneï Kroniōni.
sentences.l:
and wine from their cups to the ground they poured, nor did anyone bring himself
to drink before, before pouring a libation to the exceeding-strong son of Cronus.
sentences.i: They poured wine from their cups onto the ground, and no one could bring himself to drink before he had poured a libation to the son of Cronus, of surpassing strength.
sentences.n: Fear turns to piety: the libation before drinking. δεπάων is the epic genitive plural of δέπας ‘cup’; χαμάδις ‘to the ground’; χέον is an unaugmented imperfect of χέω ‘pour’. οὐδέ τις ἔτλη is ‘nor did anyone bring himself’ (τλάω, the house ‘bring oneself to’), with the infinitive πιέειν ‘to drink’, an epic form of πιεῖν. πρὶν … πρίν is ‘before … before’, the first an adverb with the first infinitive, the second with λεῖψαι, the aorist infinitive of λείβω ‘pour a libation’ (the Odyssey has μέθυ λεῖψαι at 12.362). ὑπερμενέϊ Κρονίωνι ‘to the exceeding-strong son of Cronus’ is Zeus, as at 7.315.

sentences.t: κοιμήσαντ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα καὶ ὕπνου δῶρον ἕλοντο.
sentences.tr: koimēsant’ ar’ epeita kai hypnou dōron helonto.
sentences.l: They lay down to sleep then, and of sleep took the gift.
sentences.i: Then they lay down to sleep and took the gift of sleep.
sentences.n: The book ends with the night’s rest, in the formula the Odyssey uses (16.481). κοιμήσαντ’ is κοιμήσαντο, the aorist middle of κοιμάω, ‘lay down to sleep’; ἄρ’ ἔπειτα ‘then’; ὕπνου δῶρον ἕλοντο ‘took the gift of sleep’, with ἕλοντο the aorist middle of αἱρέω, as in δόρπον ἕλοντο at 466. This is the last line of Book 7.
